comment.value: The paper focuses on proving under mild sufficient conditions (that normal form and Markov games satisfy)  existence of finite length satisficing paths from any initial joint strategy profile. Satisficing paths are sequences of joints strategies for which an agent does not change his strategy at time t+1 if he plays best response at time t. The result of this paper generalizes prior work by Yongacoglu (the main roadmap is similar but it seems there are a few extra ingredients in the proofs). Overall the scores indicate weak acceptance, i.e., the paper is a borderline case. There was a lot of criticism about the writeup/presentation and moreover the AC believes that the main result has limited scope. We recommend rejection with reservations.

author_final_remarks.value:
To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to extend satisfacing path theory to grouped satisfacing path theory. By investigating the topological structure of strategy sets and the partial analyticity of payoff functions, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for reducing the original game to subgames under the "win-stay, lose-shift" principle.

Drawing on existing research in satisfacing path theory, we introduce — for the first time — the well-ordering property of integer sets to prove the existence of grouped satisfacing paths, thereby circumventing the difficulties associated with direct construction in prior works. Furthermore, by exploring the relationship between different games and pure strategy games, we generalize the existence of grouped satisfacing paths from pure strategy games to different game classes.

In this process, we also provide the first solution to the existence problem of satisfacing paths in Markov games, demonstrating the broad applicability of our results.

Since the problem we study is a mathematical abstract problem derived from reinforcement learning and game theory, rigorous formalization is indispensable. This approach may sacrifice some degree of readability. However, the strict mathematical definitions and proofs ensure the validity of our conclusions.

Thank you for your response. I have re-read the paper, and now I believe the proofs are all valid and I will increase my score. But I want to clarify some points here and I strongly recommend the authors re-write sections of their proofs to be clearer. The main problem with the paper now is that it is somewhat difficult to follow the proofs, even though the conclusions are correct. This difficulty is partly because of the heavy notation but largely because the authors fluidly switch between spaces and topologies without clearly identifying when the topology has changed.

On my first question, the explanation of why (14) holds is actually more direct: if (14) does not hold, we contract the hypothesis that $s$ was a local minimum. So, (14) holds.

On my second question, I now think the set $\{ s_j \} \times C$ is not open in the original topology. The set $C$ is open in the relative topology induced in the way you describe. The statement of Lemma 1 part 2 has an error in it, as far as I can tell, in the sense that $ O \subset T_{\epsilon} (s)$ is not open in the way the reader would expect. This poses no problem for the later proofs, but it is confusing and it made me wonder whether the paper was correct.

To fix this issue in the second question, I recommend clearly explaining the topology that you are considering when making claims about openness (here and also elsewhere in the paper). In my opinion, it isn’t enough to say that a particular set is a subset of another (e.g. Line 465) or talking about domains (as you did in certain parts of your rebuttal). It would be much clearer to explicitly mention the subspace topology, for example as you did under “Mathematical fact 1” of your rebuttal.

Besides these issues in clarity, I think the proofs are all correct. Thank you for answering my other questions 4-8. With the proviso that some revision is necessary, I think this paper should be accepted.

Thank you for your detailed response. Below are some comments on your response.

* Actually the method between Line 234 and Line 242 is a new and notable technique.

I agree that this method is indeed new and has not been used in existing papers. But I think the insight here is also quite straightforward: Finding the $x^t$ that makes the satisfied players (taking non-negative integer values) minimum. The only difference is that (if my understanding is correct): this paper requires $x^t$ to be globally minimum across all possible satisfying paths, which may not be constructed in finite time but exists by nature; existing paper [39] only needs $x^t$ to be locally minimum, which can be constructed in finite time. Such a difference is not substantial in my opinion.

* To my question 1

Since the paper defines partial analyticity on partial input $x _i$ on function $f(x _i, x _{-i})$, it's natural to consider some "global analyticity property" to all inputs, i.e., $f(ap + (1-a) q)$ is an analytic function on $a$. From the proof of Corollary 3, the paper proves that the payoff function is partially analytic (and not linear generally). It seems that a similar proof would indicate that the payoff function in Corollary 3 is also "globally analytic". Since this kind of "global analyticity" seems more natural than "partial analyticity", a natural question arises: Are all partial analytical functions global analytic?

Also for the paper's clarity purpose, if these two definitions are equivalent, then it's better to use the "global analyticity" assumption for simplicity; otherwise, "partial analyticity" would become a strictly weaker requirement than "global analyticity", and the paper might benefit from clarify this; even worse, if there exists obstacles to prove or disprove the equivalence, then current version is also acceptable.

* To my question 2

Sorry for neglecting Definition 8, and I have polished my initial review w.r.t. this point.

* To authors' response to my question 3

I appreciate the authors for their response fully addressing my initial question.

However, the author's response raises another question: It seems that "each (player, state) pair follows the principle in the satisficing path" is a sufficient and necessary condition of "the player follows the principle". It is because in Markov Decision Process (MDP), let there be $m$ states and $\sigma = (\sigma _1, ..., \sigma _m)$ be the player's strategy where $\sigma _j$ maps the $j$'th state to some action. Then $\sigma$ is player's optimal strategy if and only if for all j, $\sigma _j$ is player's optimal strategy given $\sigma _{-j}$ fixed. I think this argument is still more natural than defining an alternative concept of "group satisficing path".

Based on the author does not convince me that the technical contribution over existing works is substantial enough, I've decided to maintain my positive evaluation.

Thank you for your comments! We will revise our paper to make it more standardized.

When some mathematical concepts appear in the paper, we will write down their definitions, simply explain their meanings and list reference books for readers to consult. We will make the paper more intelligible.

In Definition 4, we introduce the group concept into the satisficing path and then use mathematical formal language to express such a concept. We will rewrite these definitions to make them clearer. 

We define satisficing paths and grouped satisficing paths in mathematical formal language in order to prevent the ambiguity from occurring. We will add more intuitive explanations to help readers grasp the relationship between them.

Different kinds of games have relationships between each other. We have explained and constructed these relationships in corollaries. Using these relationships, we can extend the conclusions in pure strategy games to other kinds of games. As a result, we can achieve 4 corollaries from Theorem 2. To make these relationships clearer, we will explain them in the main text.

Question. Using grouped satisficing paths can overcome the limitation of satisficing paths, thus generalizing the results from previous works. The concept of group comes from the fact that some games are team games rather than personal games. So grouped satisficing paths can have a wider range of applications. Corollary 3 presents the advantage of grouped satisficing paths, thus proving the existence of satisficing paths in Markov games. In this proof, we construct a pure strategy game from a Markov game, thus creating (player, state) pairs. In order to keep pace with the original game, these pairs should be grouped according to players. This is the advantage of grouped satisficing paths.

Thank you for your time reviewing the paper! We will correct grammar errors. To illustrate the new ideas of our work, we will clarify the difference between this paper and previous works. We will rewrite definitions to make each one clearer.

Weakness. From high-level perspective, there are some similar ideas as in [39]. Actually, we were inspired from their insightful work. However, when we did an in-depth research on a local minimum, we found out the connection between the best response group count and the mode of the best response group [Theorem 1]. To find out what basic conditions cause such a result, we tried our best to introduce topology and analytic extendability in our research. In my opinion, the introduction of topology is the most fundamental aspect in our study, different from existing works and [39], although the majority of topological language is placed in the appendix. Actually, we get some structures of the joint strategy space by using topology [Lemma 1]. I think these methods and results may help us further our study and other people's study and let us view MARL from a different perspective. 

Another important thing is that we introduce partially analyticity or analytic functions. The importance of this technique is based on the fact that not all payoff functions in games are as simple as linear functions. Linear functions can be found in the proof in [39]. But as we see the proof of Corollary 3, the functions related to payoff functions can be somewhat complicated. So when we assume that payoff functions are partially analytic, we can deal with a wider field of games. Combining topology space with partially analyticity can help us extend local properties to global properties [Lemma 2]. 

In the proof of Theorem 2, we can only say that the technique between Line 242 and Line 250 which finds an equilibrium in a sub-game and proves the joint strategy profile is also an equilibrium, is similar to the technique in [39]. Actually the method between Line 234 and Line 242 is a new and notable technique. Usually this technique is called the well ordered set of integers. Due to this technique, we can assert the existence of the path connecting the initial joint strategy profile and a local minimum, without falling into the trouble of construction. This construction in some certain games can be found in existing works. So this technique can be used in a wider field, regardless of the mode of joint strategy. Also due to this reason, we can extend the conclusion to a pure-strategy game. 

When we talk about the applications, pure-strategy game is the role in this paper. Because we can find relationships between pure-strategy games and other kinds of games. Exploiting these relationships, we can extend the conclusion to different kinds of games, including normal games in [39] [Corollary 2]. Actually as [39] says that they cannot solve the existence problem in Markov games when the number of players is more than $3$, we can use this relationship idea to solve this problem [Corollary 3].

Question 2. When we suppose that players can only choose their strategies in the neighborhood of their current strategies, the main obstruction is in Lemma 1. We can also use the well ordered set of integers as in Theorem 2 to find a path connecting initial joint strategy profile with a local minimum. So maybe there exists something quantitative, but we do not know. In order to measure the distance between any strategy profile and some equilibrium, we maybe need some more complicated mathematical tools, like covering space or measure space etc.

Technical concern 1. There are two mathematical facts.

Mathematical fact 1. We are given the topology space $(X, T)$, where $T$ represents the collection of all open sets in $X$, and the subspace $Y \subset X$. Let $U = \{t \cap Y \mid t \in T\}$. Then $(Y, U)$ is a topological subspace, where each $u \in U$ is open in $Y$ though some of them may not be open in $X$. So when we talk about the openness of some set, we need to consider the domain. 

Mathematical fact 2. When $Y$ is open in $X$, then each $u \in U$ is also open in $X$. This means that the topology of open subspace remains its openness.

We can only say that $O \subset T_{\epsilon} (s)$ is open in $T_{\epsilon}(s)$. Let us go back to the equality (14) [Line 486]. When we say that $V\backslash A$ is open and $B_{n+i}$ is closed, this is based on the domain $V$. And when we say that $B_{n+i} \cap (V\backslash A)$ is closed, this is based on the domain $V \backslash A$. Here, we consider $V \backslash A$ as a topological subspace, using the mathematical fact 1. Since $V \backslash A$ is a Baire space when it is non-empty [Line 478], so we can apply the Baire category theorem, namely case 2 [Line 489]. So we can find out an open set $C \subset B_{n+i} \cap (V\backslash A)$ in some $B_{n+i} \cap (V\backslash A)$ while the openness of $C$ is based on the domain $V \backslash A$. This is according to the Baire category theorem. Since $V \backslash A$ is open in the domain $V$, we can say that $C$ is also open in the domain $V$. This is according to the mathematical fact 2. 

Let us go back to the last sentence [Line 492]. $T_{\epsilon} (s)$ is actually a subspace in $\prod_{i\in I} S_i$. And there is a one-to-one mapping between $T_{\epsilon} (s)$ and $V$, simply removing or adding the coordinate of $s_J$. Due to this one-to-one mapping, the openness in these two domain can be maintained under the natural definition of topological subspace. Actually the base of topology in $R^2$ is all open balls. So when we consider the base of subspace topology in the line $x=0$, namely $0 \times R$, is actually the intersections of all these open balls with this line. summary.value: The paper study learning dynamics arising by the simple principle of “win-stay, lose-shift” in pure strategy games. In particular they refine the notion of satisficing path (a sequence of strategies converging to an equilibrium and satisfying conditions encoding the principle above) to the one of group satisficing path. They first show sufficient conditions under which a group-satisficing path in finite time exists for all starting strategies in pure games. Then, as corollaries, they show the same for satisficing paths in different and more complex type of games.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Positive points**:
The topic per-se in interesting: it is well known that studying independent dynamics in MARL is non-trivial. The question of sufficient conditions is also interesting.

**Negative points**:
I think that the paper would need to be revised strongly from a presentation perspective. The english is sometimes informal or too much formal, the ‘Formalization’ section (which would be Preliminaries to me) lack a lot fo concepts that are named without any explanation in the other sections of the paper. To mention one: Baire spaces: it is very likely that many AGT researchers would either not know or remember such definition and thus it would be important to include it in the main paper, before mentioning it. Same goes for topological conditions like Haussdorff etc. On the other hand, in Definition 4, the authors redefine what a partition is! The difference between the group satisficing paths definition and the satisficing paths ones should be discussed a bit more in depth since they are very similar. Also, I think that the authors mix a lot in the presentation between pure games and Markov games and in general, models for MARL and that is very confusing.
All in all the paper is not ready for acceptance, in my opinion.

summary.value:
This paper considers a problem in game theory about the reachability of equilibrium points through a process related to “win-stay, lose-shift” strategy updates. The authors address open questions from a recent work [39] and show that the reachability results of [39] extend to a larger class of games that are relevant to multi-agent reinforcement learning.

The techniques used in this paper generalize the existing definition of “satisficing paths” to “grouped satisficing paths”, which encompass multi-agent coalitions, with the special case of single agent coalitions recovering the original definition. The authors study the existence of grouped satisficing paths to equilibrium by studying the topological properties of such paths, defining a notion of local minimum for the set of strategies and drawing conclusions about what this means for coalitions that are best responding at such a local minimum.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths: 

The topic covered here seems fundamental to game theory and multi-agent reinforcement learning. I have some concerns about the proofs of some lemmas and Theorem 1, but if they are correct (or if they can be fixed), the main result of this paper contributes nicely to this research area. 

Specifically, Theorem 2 and Corollary 4 are good contributions. The authors generalize the best previously known result, going from finite games and special cases of Markov games to general Markov games.

In addition to finding more general results, the analytic techniques used are interesting, as they translate some ideas and analysis present in the earlier papers [39] and [40] into topological language and pave the way for applying new tools to understand the game theoretic landscape.  Some caveats to this strength will be described in the weaknesses section, but these caveats might be easy to fix.


Weaknesses:

This paper’s main weakness is about the proofs of Lemmas 1 and 2, which may or may not be correct (or fixable) but left me with some concerns. These are outlined below. If these concerns about the topological proofs can be addressed in the discussion period, then I will raise my score. If the issues seem to persist after the discussion, I may lower my score. Some secondary weaknesses include how the paper cites existing work and small issues in the writing. 

Technical concern 1: The openness of $O \subset T_{\epsilon} ( s )$ in part 2 of Lemma 1 hasn’t been proven to my liking. It may still be true, but I’d like some clarification and probably some re-writing. My issues are with equality (14) and the final sentence of the proof of Lemma 1. Please see the associated questions.

Technical concern 2: How can we be sure that the open set $O \subset U \subset \prod_{i \in I} S_i $ in Lemma 2’s proof can be decomposed into the product of open sets $O = \prod_{i \in I} O_i $ with each $O_i \subset S_i$ an open set. I think $O$ can be written as an arbitrary (i.e. possibly uncountable) union of such product sets, but it’s not clear to me why we can do it using a single product as claimed in equation (15). Consider, for example, the following open set in the plane {$ (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : 0<x<1  \text{ and } x < y < x + 1 $}. This is open in $\mathbb{R}^2$ but I don't think you can write it as $O_1 \times O_2$ where $O_1, O_2 \subset \mathbb{R}$ are open sets. In game theoretic terms, these constraints relating allowable values of x and y are interdependent, meaning that the strategies of each player shouldn’t be arbitrary but should depend on $s_{-k}$, no? In short, I'm skeptical that $t_k$ can therefore be truly arbitrarily chosen, and Lemma 2 may have a flaw. I’m not saying it’s certainly incorrect, but I need to be convinced.

Outside of these technical concerns, there are secondary weaknesses related to how this paper contextualizes itself in the literature. If I am understanding the proofs of this paper and the preceding works [39] and [40] correctly, the main line of argument used in this paper basically mirrors earlier lines of argument to a large extent. This point should probably be acknowledged more clearly, since it better explains how the innovation of this paper is its analytic techniques studying the local minima in more complex game settings. For example, it appears that Markov games were also discussed in [40], and a two-player result for Markov games was obtained using basically the same line of argument as used here. The analysis of the present paper captures the case where $| I | \geq 3$ in a way that [40]’s analysis did not, which is certainly a strength, but in my opinion it’s worth clarifying.

Related to the point above, the authors may wish to cite another paper by the authors of [39], which seems to relate to the idea of well-defined sub-games used in Theorem 2 of this paper. The paper: B. Yongacoglu, G. Arslan, L. Pavel and S. Yüksel, "Generalizing Better Response Paths and Weakly Acyclic Games," 2024 IEEE 63rd Conference on Decision and Control (CDC), 2024, pp. 5262-5267. 

Besides the points above about the topological proofs and the literature, I think the abstract and first paragraph of this paper should probably be re-written. In their current state, they parallel the abstract and first paragraph of [39] to an alarming degree. The remainder of the paper and technical findings are sufficiently different that this is only a minor weakness, in my opinion. 


Minor notes:
- Definition 8 has some minor grammatical issues.
- Line 239 says “Reduction to absurdity needs to be used here”. If this is intentional, I’d recommend re-writing it for style. There are other somewhat awkward phrases as well as some grammatical issues elsewhere in this proof.
- While not a mistake in the strict sense, the symbol $x$ is used inconsistently, which was a bit distracting. In some places, $x$ was an integer (e.g. proof of Theorem 2), in others $x$ was a strategy, in others (e.g. equation (13)) $x$ was a player, in others $x$ was a real number in [0,1] (Line 507, equation (16)), and in still others $x$ was a state for a Markov game (p. 18, Line 568). 
- Similar to the last point, the sets $A$ and $A_k$ were used with several unrelated meanings, which was also a bit distracting.

1. (Resolved) Can you explain the equality in (14)? I don’t see why this follows from the previous sentence.

2. (Resolved) In Line 496, you say “Obviously, $s_J \times C $ is an open set in $T_{\epsilon} (s)$”. But even if $C$ is an open set, $s_J$ is only a singleton — how can this be open in the topology of the ambient space (where players in J can also vary their strategies)?

summary.value: This paper introduces the concept of a "grouped satisficing path", which extends the existing game-theoretic concept of a "satisficing path" (one in which strategies that are already best responses don't change). It studies the properties of this grouped satisficing path from a topological perspective. Finally, it proves sufficient conditions for the existence of such a path from any initial strategy profile to some equilibrium. This supplements existing research on convergence in MARL, and provides theoretical support for stochastic update approaches.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
The theoretical result looks interesting and relevant, and seems to have fairly wide applicability (per the 4 corollaries on page 8).

The grammar and phrasing used in the paper could be improved at some points, which I've described below. This also contains a few points where clarity could be improved. Since the term "best response" is used very often, sometimes multiple times in the same sentence, I suggest shortening it to "BR" (after introducing the acronym somewhere near the beginning of the paper.)

I also suggest amending the somewhat-awkward phrase "has achieved best response" to simply "is a best response", and future tenses ("will") to present tenses ("is"). Mathematics is usually written in an atemporal/timeless way, and usually reads better that way.

Example to illustrate (from page 6):

- Before: "the group which has achieved best response in $s$ will still achieve best response in $t$."

- After: "the group that is a BR in $s$ is still a BR in $t$."

I suggest improving the structure/presentation of the argument on page 7. Perhaps it can be broken down into smaller, clearly-labeled pieces. This also makes it clearer which assumptions are applicable to which parts. For example, if one is doing a sub-proof by contradiction (from a false assumption), the end of that sub-proof should be clearly marked.

I also suggest using singular instead of plural, wherever possible. It's easier to contemplate a single object in mind at a time, rather than multiple objects, especially when juggling multiple quantifiers. Example (from page 7):

- Before: any player does not change their strategies

summary.value:
A satisfying path is a sequence of strategy profiles such that 1) any player with best response strategy in some time does not update her strategy in next time, and 2) ends with an NE. Existing work[39] proves the existence of satisfying path with arbitrary initial point in a finite-player, finite-action (allowing mixed NE), normal-form game.

This work generalizes the result to a class of games with many theoretical assumptions. Among them, (I think) the most insightful assumptions are: 1) the payoff function is partially analytic, 2) any sub-game exhibits an NE.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths**:

The problem studied is well-motivated. The insights behind all results are clearly explained. The generalization over finite-action games is a theoretical contribution.

**Weaknesses**:

1. I think the most crucial weakness is that the techniques used in this paper are similar to those in [39], which makes the contribution of this paper seemingly incremental. There indeed exist some new techniques, such as the usage of Baire category theorem to justify the existence of an inner point in a set (Lemma 1). However, I found the high-level idea similar: 1) find $x^ t$ that makes the satisfied players minimum; 2) find the NE $x^ *$ of sub-game with unsatisfied players; 3) prove that the strategy profile $x^ {t+1}$, which equals $x^ t$ for satisfied players and $x^ *$ for unsatisfied players, substitutes an NE and is a feasible successor of $x^ t$. I would like to increase my score if (part of) the techniques used to prove the main result were found essentially different from existing works, especially [39].

2. Some sentences have grammar flaws, such as:

* line 163 "while maximum means cannot increase"
* line 205-208, "... will (not/still) achieve"
* line 517 "a important"

3. See questions below.

questions.value:
I would appreciate if the authors could response following questions:

1. Since partial analytic assumption seems unnatural, I have some questions w.r.t this assumption:

* Does there exist some functions which is continuous, partially analytic but not (globally) analytic?
* Does there exist some games that exhibit at least one NE, but fail to have a satisfying path with some initial point (probably violating partial analytic property)?

2. (Resolved) What is the precise definition of "sub-game"? This concept appears in the statements of Theorem 2 but the authors give no definition before. Though it is not hard to speculate the definition of "sub-game", a precise definition before its first usage would improve the clarity.

3. I'm also confused about the concept of "grouped satisfaction path" over "(individual) satisfaction path" as in [39]. The author claims that this concept is useful in the proof of Corollary 3. In the proof, the author first construct a new pure-strategy game $H$, in which the players in the new game consist of all $(i,x)$ pair where $i$ is a player and $x$ is a state in the original Markov game $G$. A group set $A$ is used to construct the existence of NE in any sub-game of $H$. However, since any sub-game of $H$ is exactly a Markov game with singleton action set in some (player, state) pair, the existence of NE should be natural, which might then indicate the concept of "grouped satisfaction path" is unnecessary.

final_justification.value: This paper investigates an interesting generalization of existing results (e.g., [39]) from basic topological assumptions. The technical roadmap follows that of [39] at a high level, but part of technical steps are new. One indication of this paper's result is that any (finite-state, finite-action) Markov Game exhibits a satisficing path, which is not a direct consequence of existing papers. Due to these reasons, I think the paper's contribution is above the acceptance threshold.

title.value: Grouped Satisficing Paths in Pure Strategy Games: a Topological Perspective

TLDR.value: We study the topological properties of the grouped satisficing paths and prove that such paths to equilibrium exist in N-player games and finite-state Markov games.

abstract.value: In game theory and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), each agent selects a strategy, interacts with the environment and other agents, and subsequently updates its strategy based on the received payoff. This process generates a sequence of joint strategies $(s^t)_{t \geq 0}$, where $s^t$ represents the strategy profile of all agents at time step $t$. A widely adopted principle in MARL algorithms is "win-stay, lose-shift", which dictates that an agent retains its current strategy if it achieves the best response. This principle exhibits a fixed-point property when the joint strategy has become an equilibrium. The sequence of joint strategies under this principle is referred to as a satisficing path, a concept first introduced in [40] and explored in the context of $N$-player games in [39]. A fundamental question arises regarding this principle: Under what conditions does every initial joint strategy $s$ admit a finite-length satisficing path $(s^t)_{0 \leq t \leq T}$ where $s^0=s$ and $s^T$ is an equilibrium? This paper establishes a sufficient condition for such a property, and demonstrates that any finite-state Markov game, as well as any $N$-player game, guarantees the existence of a finite-length satisficing path from an arbitrary initial strategy to some equilibrium. These results provide a stronger theoretical foundation for the design of MARL algorithms.
